title: Albaloo polo
subtitle: Persian sour cherry rice with saffron chicken
excerpt: Albaloo polo is a Persian rice dish in which tart dried cherries are layered with saffron-stained basmati to create a beautiful, sweet-sour combination. Whole saffron chicken pieces nestle in the rice as it steams to a crisp-bottomed tahdig. It is one of the showstoppers of Persian home cooking.
sourceNotes: A classic Persian fruit rice (polo). Albaloo means sour cherry in Persian. The dish is made with fresh or dried sour cherries; dried cranberries are the closest widely available UK substitute.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The chicken marinade can be applied the day before. The rice is best cooked and served fresh.

content.text: Albaloo polo is a Persian fruit rice: sour cherries and saffron-stained basmati are layered in alternating colours and steamed together. The result is a dish with real visual beauty and a flavour that is at once rich, tart, and floral.
The tart cherry cuts through the richness of the saffron chicken, and the crisp tahdig base gives a textural contrast that makes every mouthful satisfying. This is a centrepiece dish.

Dried sour cherries (albaloo) are available in Iranian or Persian grocery shops. Dried cranberries are the closest common substitute; they are sharper and slightly less complex but work well. Soak whichever you use in warm water for 15 minutes to plump them before using.

items.prepNote: or dried sour cherries (albaloo) if available, soaked 15 minutes in warm water

content.text: Melt the butter in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft and golden. Season the chicken with salt. Add the chicken pieces and brown for 4 minutes each side. Pour over half the saffron water, cover, and cook on a low heat for 35 minutes until the chicken is cooked through. Keep warm.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Drain the soaked rice and add to the boiling water. Cook for 6 to 7 minutes until the rice is about two-thirds cooked: firm in the centre but no longer chalky on the outside. Drain well and rinse with cold water to stop the cooking.

Melt the butter in a heavy-based pot over medium heat. Mix 2 tbsp of yoghurt with 2 large spoonfuls of parboiled rice and spread over the base to form the tahdig layer. Mix the drained cherries with the cinnamon and remaining saffron water. Alternate layers of rice and cherries in the pot, mounding towards the top. Drape a clean tea towel under the lid to absorb steam, and cook on a low heat for 40 to 45 minutes until the base is golden and crisp. To serve, invert the rice onto a large plate so the tahdig crust is on top.

rows.cause: Heat too high or wrong pot material
rows.fix: Use the lowest possible heat after the initial 5 minutes. A heavy-based or non-stick pot works best.
Parboil only until just two-thirds cooked; it will finish in the steam. Rinse with cold water immediately after draining.

rows.symptom: Rice not cooked through after steaming
rows.cause: Lid not sealed tightly or heat too low
rows.fix: The tea-towel lid is essential. If the rice feels underdone at 40 minutes, add 2 tbsp of hot water around the sides and continue for 10 more minutes.

content.text: Replace the chicken with lamb pieces simmered until tender. Some versions of the cherry polo include a small amount of sugar added to the cherries to balance their tartness; taste the cranberries and adjust accordingly. Zereshk polo (the barberry version) uses dried barberries instead of sour cherries and is perhaps the most famous fruit polo.
The chicken can be cooked a day ahead and reheated gently. The polo itself is best made and served fresh; the tahdig will not remain crisp once refrigerated.

Fruit polos are a hallmark of Persian festive cooking. Albaloo polo appears at Nowruz (Persian New Year) celebrations, at weddings, and at large family gatherings. The combination of sour fruit with saffron rice is distinctly Persian and has no real parallel in other rice-cooking traditions.
